facts.claim: "The Warrior" was written by Holly Knight and Nick Gilder and produced by Mike Chapman. It was the lead single from Scandal's 1984 album Warrior, credited as Scandal featuring Patty Smyth.
Warrior was recorded at The Record Plant in New York City between August 1983 and January 1984. Some recording was also done at MCA-Whitney Studios in Glendale.

Album credits list Patty Smyth on vocals, Zack Smith and Keith Mack on guitars and backing vocals, Ivan Elias on bass, Thommy Price on drums and backing vocals, and Peter Wood on synthesizer. William Wittman engineered and mixed.
Patty Smyth said producer Mike Chapman, who also wrote with Holly Knight, brought the band "The Warrior". Smyth did not write it.
Patty Smyth loved the song and knew it was a hit. It reached #1 on the rock charts and #7 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Smyth said she was pressured into a concept video she didn't want and begged the label not to release it. She had wanted a live performance video. It became a Top 20 video of 1984.
Smyth said in the book I Want My MTV that she was crestfallen when she saw the video. She said she had no idea it would look like an off-Broadway production of Cats.
Holly Knight said she had never realised how much the warrior spirit was inside her before writing the song. She described it as standing up for what you believe in and following through.

Warrior was Scandal's debut and only full-length studio album. "The Warrior" became the band's biggest hit, and the album was certified platinum. Smyth left the group soon afterwards and the band broke up.
Scandal's first release was the 1982 EP Scandal, which included "Goodbye to You". By the time the Warrior tour hit the road in 1984, only Smyth and Keith Mack remained from the original lineup.

research.lineage: The song is mid-1980s synth-and-guitar pop rock written by Holly Knight, who also wrote "Love Is a Battlefield" with Chapman. It sits in the same MTV-era radio-rock lane as Pat Benatar, The Cars and Foreigner.

draft:
The whole bargain of **"The Warrior"** hangs on three words tucked into the chorus: "If you survive." The song sounds like a victory lap, all swagger and stacked harmonies, but the promise it makes comes with conditions. Heart-to-heart you'll win, Patty Smyth tells the person she's chasing, and then she adds the catch. Love here isn't shelter. It's a test you might not pass.

The verses play out as a hunt. Smyth's narrator watches someone running from their own heart, calls out their hunger, and dares them to break loose. Then the frame flips: "Who's the hunter, who's the game?" That question is the song's most honest moment. For all the chest-out bravado, the singer doesn't know who's in control, and the wanting runs both ways. The key image, "Shootin' at the walls of heartache," says even more. The gunfire isn't aimed at a lover. It's aimed at the hurt itself, the kind of fight you only pick once you've already been wounded. The pride and the pain never settle into one feeling, and the song doesn't try to make them.

Holly Knight and Nick Gilder wrote it, and producer Mike Chapman, who'd written with Knight before, brought it to the band. Knight later said she hadn't realised how much warrior spirit was in her until she wrote it. To her, that spirit meant standing up for what you believe in and following through. Smyth didn't write a word, but she loved it and knew it was a hit. It went to number one on the rock charts and number seven on the Billboard Hot 100.

The record, cut largely at the Record Plant in New York, earns that confidence. Thommy Price's kick, snare and hi-hat lock in with Ivan Elias's bass for a driving mid-tempo push. The guitars from Zack Smith and Keith Mack shift between a clean arpeggiated figure and big sustained chords. Peter Wood's synth pad fills the space underneath. Smyth's voice is clear and strong. The backing vocals move in parallel with her, thickening the lines they want you to shout back. It's polished, full and built for radio, squarely in the lane of Pat Benatar, The Cars and Foreigner. Knight also co-wrote "Love Is a Battlefield" with Chapman, and the titles alone tell you she was working the same idea: romance as combat.

The song outgrew its costume. Smyth wanted a live performance video and got a concept piece she begged the label not to release. She said it looked like an off-Broadway production of *Cats*. It's a nice irony that a song about refusing to be tamed got dressed up anyway. Warrior was Scandal's only full-length album, and Smyth left soon after.

It sticks because it lets you feel armored and exposed in the same breath, swinging at heartache while admitting out loud that you might not make it through.
